deep.reconstruction:
Context: this folio is a draft of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (written 1854, published posthumously by Dedekind in 1867). It contains the end of the historical section (§3 of the printed text), the opening of Part II, and the start of §4, 'Über den Begriff eines bestimmten Integrals und den Umfang seiner Gültigkeit'.

(A) Historical critique, no mathematics.
- Dirksen (Crelle 4, p.170) worked apparently without knowing Dirichlet's paper. Riemann says Dirksen's approach is broadly right but inexact in details:
  - In one special case he gets a wrong value for the sum of the series (margin: 'l.c. Formel 22').
  - In a side argument he relies on a series expansion that is not always possible (margin: 'l.c. art. 3').
  - Consequently his proof is complete only for functions whose first derivative is finite everywhere.
- Bessel (margin: Schumacher's Astronomische Nachrichten Bd. 16, Nr. 374, 21 March 1839) tried to simplify Dirichlet's proof. Riemann judges that his changes simplify nothing essential in the reasoning. At most they fix the ideas more concretely and allow a more convenient view (the inserted phrase), while rigour and generality suffer considerably.
- Conclusion: no investigation yet covers all functions representable by trigonometric series. Part II of this work attempts one.

(B) Programme of Part II (bracketed paragraph).
- Earlier work aimed to prove the Fourier series for functions occurring in nature. It could therefore start from an arbitrary f and impose whatever restrictions the proof needed.
- Riemann's aim requires the converse question: if f(x) = A_0 + Σ (a_n cos nx + b_n sin nx), what follows about the behaviour of f, i.e. how its value changes as the argument varies continuously?
- Because the analysis rests on foundations of the definite integral, he first fixes the concept of the integral and its range of validity.

(C) Definition of the (Riemann) integral.
1. Take a partition a = x_0 < x_1 < ... < x_{n-1} < x_n = b.
2. Set δ_i = x_i − x_{i−1}, so δ_1 = x_1 − a, ..., δ_n = b − x_{n−1}.
3. Let ε_i ∈ (0,1) be positive proper fractions ('positive ächte Brüche').
4. Form S = Σ_{i=1}^n δ_i f(x_{i−1} + ε_i δ_i). The tag x_{i−1} + ε_i δ_i is an arbitrary interior point of the i-th subinterval.
5. S depends on the choice of the δ's and ε's.
6. If S approaches a fixed limit A as max δ_i → 0, whatever the δ's and ε's, then A =: ∫_a^b f(x) dx.
   - Modern form: for every η > 0 there is d > 0 such that |S − A| < η for every tagged partition of mesh < d.
7. Otherwise the symbol has no meaning in this strict sense.

(D) Extension to an interior singularity. The margin text replaces the body text here.
- Suppose f becomes infinite as x approaches a single point c in (a,b).
- Then S has no limit: whatever smallness is prescribed for the δ's, S can be given any value. [My gloss: choose the tag in a subinterval near c where |f| is arbitrarily large.]
- So in the strict sense the integral is meaningless.
- One extension accepted by all mathematicians, completed on the next page: ∫_a^b f = lim_{α_1, α_2 → 0} ( ∫_a^{c−α_1} f + ∫_{c+α_2}^b f ), with α_1 and α_2 tending to 0 independently, if this limit exists.
- On the next page Cauchy's further conventions (e.g. the principal value, α_1 = α_2) are rejected as arbitrary.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page.

The claim that S can take 'any value' when f is unbounded near c is slightly loose. It is literally true if f takes arbitrarily large values of both signs. If f → +∞ only, S can be made arbitrarily large positive but not arbitrarily negative. What actually matters, absence of a limit (S unbounded), holds in any case.
For S to have a limit, f must be bounded (the next page uses this explicitly). That is the real point behind the remark about unbounded f.
The phrase 'durch ε einen positiven ächten Bruch' uses a single ε, but the formula uses individual ε_1, ..., ε_n. This is a notational slip in the draft; the printed version uses separate ε_i.

results.what: Critique of Dirksen's and Bessel's work on Fourier series relative to Dirichlet (1829)
results.modern_name: historical assessment of convergence proofs for Fourier series

results.what: Formulating the converse problem: what properties must a function representable by a trigonometric series have?
results.modern_name: representation/uniqueness problem for general trigonometric series (Riemann's theory of trigonometric series)

results.what: Definition of the definite integral as the limit of tagged sums Σ δ_i f(x_{i−1}+ε_i δ_i) as the mesh → 0, independent of the tags
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1854 (published 1867); Cauchy 1823 used left-endpoint sums for continuous functions

results.what: Improper integral across an interior singularity as a two-sided limit with independent α_1, α_2
results.modern_name: improper Riemann integral (as opposed to Cauchy principal value)
results.usually_credited_to: Cauchy (1820s); Riemann's formulation in the Habilitationsschrift

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of the published Habilitationsschrift (§3 and the opening of §4). The text nearly matches the printed version, including the definition of the Riemann integral and the improper integral. Only minor draft wording differences (e.g. the inserted phrase about a 'more convenient view') are new.

checkable.asserts: Riemann sums of x^2 on [0,1] with tags x_{k-1}+ε δ (ε=1/2) converge to the integral 1/3
The improper integral of 1/sqrt|x| over [-1,1] with independent limits α1, α2 → 0 exists and equals 4
For 1/x on [-1,1] the two-sided expression equals log(α1/α2), so it has no limit as α1, α2 → 0 independently (Riemann's definition gives no value), although the principal value α1=α2 gives 0
For f=1/sqrt|x| near c=0, a single term δ f(tag) with δ=1/n and tag 1/n^4 is unbounded, so the Riemann sums S have no limit even though the improper integral exists

transcription_corrections: 'Lipschitz sucht den Dirichlet'schen Beweis zu vereinfachen' should read 'Bessel sucht den Dirichlet'schen Beweis zu vereinfachen'. The marginal citation (Schumacher's Astronomische Nachrichten Bd. 16, Nr. 374, 1839) is Bessel's paper; the previous page announces Dirksen and Bessel; and the printed Habilitationsschrift has 'Bessel' here.
The marginal citation should read 'Schumacher's Astronomische Nachrichten Bd. 16. pag. 229 (N. 374) vom 21. März 1839' (page 229, issue number 374), not 'Nr. 229'.

'Wenn eine Function durch eine Function [?] durch eine trigonometrische Reihe darstellbar ist' should read 'Wenn eine Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe darstellbar ist'. The second 'durch eine Function' is a dittography of the transcription, not a meaningful phrase.
'und ∫ fx dx hätte [?] nach dem Obigen keine Bedeutung haben' is ungrammatical; most likely read 'kann nach dem Obigen keine Bedeutung haben' (printed text: 'würde ... keine Bedeutung haben').

In the struck passage, read 'Unter diesen Erweiterungen des Begriffs des bestimmten Integrals ist nur folgende ...'. The insertion above the line is 'eine' or 'diese', giving roughly '... ist diese von allen Mathematikern angenommen'.

The marginal addition near the bottom (an asterisk replacing the struck word 'Arguments', with 'f(x)' and 'in dem Intervalle (a, b)') is Riemann's replacement wording for the body text 'Wenn nämlich der Werth von fx bei der Annäherung an einen einzelnen Punkt c ...'. It should be placed accordingly.
The '70' at the right edge is the folio number.
